title: Only 6% Of Adults Can Pass This Barrister Entrance Exam
summary: Explore legal reasoning and advocacy through clues, practical situations and fresh challenges.

landing.intro:
Can you follow the evidence?
Make your strongest case.

about.body: Connect the facts, notice the details and test your understanding of legal reasoning and advocacy. Each checkpoint reveals your topic profile before a different challenge begins.

steps: Read the clues and choose one answer.
See your topic profile at each checkpoint and continue to a new challenge.
Reveal your overall result, then optionally review the answers you missed.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This is not a bar admission exam, legal qualification or legal advice. Laws and professional rules vary by jurisdiction.

stage-10.preAdCopy: Did you reach 80%? Your score and strengths are ready.

score.passed: You passed this courtroom reasoning quiz!

insights.overview: Your courtroom score at a glance

barrister-s1q1.question: What is the main purpose of presenting evidence in a hearing?

answers.a1: To replace the issue being decided
answers.a4: To reward the longest speech

barrister-s1q2.question: What is a witness generally asked to describe?

answers.a1: Information relevant to the matter being examined
answers.a2: Only what the advocate wishes were true
answers.a4: Private guesses presented as direct observation

barrister-s1q3.question: What is cross-examination in an adversarial hearing?

answers.a1: Writing the judge’s decision
answers.a2: Questioning a witness called by another party
answers.a4: Selecting the furniture

answers.a1: Every open invitation to describe an event
answers.a2: A question that suggests its desired answer
answers.a3: A question that has no words
answers.a4: Any question asked first

barrister-s1q5.question: What is the difference between an allegation and a finding?

answers.a1: A finding is only a rumour
answers.a2: An allegation is a claim; a finding is a determination after consideration
answers.a3: An allegation automatically proves a fact
answers.a4: They always mean exactly the same thing

barrister-s1q6.question: What should a closing argument connect?

answers.a1: The relevant evidence and the applicable issues or rules
answers.a4: Claims deliberately hidden from the record

barrister-s1q7.question: A witness did not see an event but heard about it later. What distinction matters?

answers.a1: No distinction can ever matter
answers.a2: Only the colour of the witness’s clothes
answers.a4: First-hand observation versus information from someone else

barrister-s2q1.question: Two people give different times for the same event. What is the best next step?

answers.a1: Choose the more confident speaker automatically
answers.a2: Average the times and call that a fact
answers.a3: Check each account against other reliable information
answers.a4: Delete both accounts without checking

barrister-s2q2.question: Which statement records an observation rather than an assumption about motive?

answers.a1: The person never cared about the meeting
answers.a2: The person intended to mislead everyone
answers.a3: The person left the room at 14:10
answers.a4: The person left because they were guilty

barrister-s2q3.question: A photograph has no known date or location. What should be checked before relying on it?

answers.a1: Whether its colours are attractive
answers.a2: Whether it matches a preferred conclusion
answers.a4: How many people like it

barrister-s2q4.question: A claim is repeated by three websites, all quoting one unnamed source. What does that show?

answers.a1: Repeated reporting, not three independent confirmations
answers.a3: Proof that no further checking is needed
answers.a4: Proof that the claim is accurate

barrister-s2q5.question: All authorised visitors have a pass. Mira has a pass. What follows from that rule alone?

answers.a1: No authorised visitors have passes
answers.a2: Mira must be an authorised visitor
answers.a3: Mira cannot be an authorised visitor
answers.a4: It does not prove Mira is an authorised visitor

barrister-s2q6.question: A new reliable fact contradicts your initial explanation. What is the sound response?

answers.a1: Treat your first idea as unchangeable
answers.a4: Change the fact to fit the explanation

barrister-s2q7.question: A report says an event happened after a change. Does that timing alone prove the change caused it?

answers.a1: Yes; if the report is long enough
answers.a4: No; earlier events can never cause later ones

barrister-s3q1.question: In a precedent-based exercise, why compare material facts between cases?

answers.a1: To avoid reading the rule
answers.a2: To assess whether the earlier reasoning applies
answers.a3: To ensure the names are identical
answers.a4: To choose the oldest document automatically

barrister-s3q2.question: A hypothetical rule prohibits vehicles except emergency vehicles on duty. Which is expressly excepted?

answers.a1: An emergency vehicle on duty
answers.a4: Any vehicle with bright paint

barrister-s3q3.question: A rule requires written notice at least 5 days before a meeting. Notice is given 2 days before. Does it satisfy the stated timing rule?

answers.a1: The rule requires no notice
answers.a3: No, the notice is too late
answers.a4: Yes, any notice is sufficient

barrister-s3q4.question: An earlier decision concerns a signed contract. A new case concerns an unsigned draft. What may matter?

answers.a1: Only whether the paper sizes match
answers.a3: Whether the signature difference is material to the reasoning
answers.a4: Nothing; all documents are legally identical

barrister-s3q5.question: What does distinguishing a precedent involve?

answers.a1: Explaining a relevant difference that limits its application
answers.a2: Pretending the decision does not exist
answers.a4: Using its title without reading it

barrister-s3q6.question: A supplied rule says an appeal must be filed by 16:00. It is filed at 16:20 with no stated exception. What follows in this exercise?

answers.a1: It misses the stated deadline
answers.a4: The deadline has no meaning

barrister-s3q7.question: A case summary omits the reason for the decision. What is most useful to examine next?

answers.a1: An unrelated opinion with no source
answers.a2: Only the font used in the summary
answers.a3: Only the number of people who shared it
answers.a4: The court’s reasoning in the decision itself

barrister-s4q1.question: Which question invites a person to describe an event in their own words?

answers.a1: “It happened exactly as I said, correct?”
answers.a4: “You were angry, weren’t you?”

barrister-s4q2.question: Someone pauses while describing a difficult event. What is a useful response?

answers.a1: Treat the pause as proof of dishonesty
answers.a2: Ask several unrelated questions at once
answers.a3: Allow time and offer a calm opportunity to continue
answers.a4: Immediately fill in the missing details

answers.a1: Agreeing with every statement automatically
answers.a2: Speaking more loudly than the other person
answers.a3: Planning your next speech while ignoring the answer
answers.a4: Paying attention and checking your understanding

barrister-s4q4.question: A term is unfamiliar to the listener. What helps?

answers.a1: Assume silence proves understanding
answers.a2: Explain it using clear, familiar words
answers.a4: Make the explanation deliberately longer

barrister-s4q5.question: Two people use the same word differently. What should be clarified?

answers.a1: Which word is longest
answers.a3: What each person means by the word
answers.a4: Nothing; identical words always mean identical ideas

barrister-s4q6.question: Which response checks understanding without assuming agreement?

answers.a1: “There is no need to explain further”
answers.a4: “Have I understood your concern correctly?”

barrister-s4q7.question: A language barrier affects an important discussion. What is the strongest support?

answers.a1: Replacing every sentence with abbreviations
answers.a2: Using a child to translate sensitive details
answers.a4: Guessing from gestures alone

barrister-s5q1.question: A decision affects a close friend. What should a professional recognise?

answers.a1: A guarantee of impartiality
answers.a4: A reason to hide the relationship

barrister-s5q2.question: Which approach treats comparable cases fairly?

answers.a1: Change criteria after seeing each person’s name
answers.a3: Use appearance as the only criterion
answers.a4: Apply relevant criteria consistently and consider relevant differences

barrister-s5q3.question: A private record is useful for a task. What should determine access?

answers.a1: Whether the file is easy to open
answers.a3: Whether the person is well known
answers.a4: Authorised purpose and applicable access rules

barrister-s5q4.question: You discover an error in your own report. What supports accountability?

answers.a1: Delete supporting records
answers.a2: Correct it transparently through the appropriate process
answers.a3: Leave it because nobody has noticed
answers.a4: Quietly blame another person

barrister-s5q5.question: What does informed agreement require in a meaningful discussion?

answers.a1: A signature without any explanation
answers.a2: A decision made by an unrelated observer
answers.a3: Relevant information and an opportunity to understand and choose
answers.a4: A promise that questions are forbidden

barrister-s5q6.question: A gift could influence a professional decision. What is the appropriate response?

answers.a1: Follow the conflict-of-interest and gifts policy
answers.a2: Hide the gift from the record
answers.a4: Promise favourable treatment

barrister-s5q7.question: A rule applies to everyone in a process. A popular person asks for a private exception. What is appropriate?

answers.a1: Use the authorised process for any exception
answers.a3: Change the rule only for that person without explanation
answers.a4: Grant it without recording the reason

barrister-s6q1.question: Two records describe the same event but give different dates. What should be done?

answers.a1: Check the discrepancy against reliable original information
answers.a2: Average the dates and treat that as verified
answers.a4: Choose the later date automatically

barrister-s6q2.question: Which note separates a statement from a verified fact?

answers.a1: “Everyone knows what happened”
answers.a2: “Lee reports that the door was open; this has not yet been checked”
answers.a3: “No check is needed because the story is detailed”
answers.a4: “The door was certainly open because Lee said so”

answers.a1: So its source can be assessed and followed up
answers.a2: To make all information automatically true
answers.a3: To prove every source is independent
answers.a4: To remove the need for dates

barrister-s6q4.question: A document is a draft. What does that mean?

answers.a1: It is necessarily false
answers.a2: It may still change before being finalised
answers.a4: Every statement has been legally certified

barrister-s6q5.question: A file has been revised several times. What helps identify the current version?

answers.a1: Whichever copy is easiest to find
answers.a2: A clear version and approval record
answers.a4: The most attractive font

barrister-s6q6.question: An entry is missing from a record. What does that establish by itself?

answers.a1: The information is not recorded there
answers.a2: The event definitely did not happen
answers.a4: The event definitely happened

barrister-s6q7.question: Why preserve an original record when making an authorised correction?

answers.a1: To guarantee the original was correct
answers.a3: To make the record harder to understand
answers.a4: To prevent anyone seeing the correction

barrister-s7q1.question: A rule says: only members may enter. Sam is not a member. What follows under that rule?

answers.a1: Sam may not enter
answers.a2: Sam may enter if the queue is short
answers.a3: The rule says nothing about Sam
answers.a4: Sam must be admitted first

barrister-s7q2.question: Every approved application has a signature. This application has no signature. What follows?

answers.a1: It is automatically approved
answers.a4: It is not approved under the stated rule

barrister-s7q3.question: A service opens only on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Which day is definitely excluded?

answers.a1: Tuesday
answers.a4: Monday

barrister-s7q4.question: Either Room A or Room B is booked, but not both. Room A is booked. What follows?

answers.a1: Room B is also booked
answers.a4: Neither room is booked

barrister-s7q5.question: A rule requires both a form and proof of identity. Only the form is present. What is missing?

answers.a1: A document not mentioned in the rule
answers.a4: A second copy of the form

barrister-s7q6.question: A policy says every urgent request is reviewed today. This request was reviewed today. What can you conclude?

answers.a1: It cannot have been urgent
answers.a4: It may or may not have been urgent

barrister-s7q7.question: Three meetings happen in order: Ana before Bo, and Bo before Cam. Who meets last?

answers.a1: Cam
answers.a4: The order cannot be determined

barrister-s8q1.question: A supply box holds 24 items. Six are used. What fraction remains?

answers.a1: One third
answers.a4: Three quarters

barrister-s8q2.question: A task begins at 14:35 and lasts 50 minutes. When does it finish?

barrister-s8q3.question: Four equal groups share 36 items. How many items are in each group?

barrister-s8q4.question: A reading rises from 40 to 50. What is the percentage increase?

barrister-s8q5.question: A plan uses a scale of 1 cm to 2 m. What distance does 6 cm represent?

answers.a1: 8 m

barrister-s8q6.question: Three loads weigh 12 kg, 15 kg and 18 kg. What is their total mass?

answers.a1: 35 kg
answers.a4: 45 kg

barrister-s8q7.question: A checklist has 20 items. Four remain unchecked. What percentage is complete?

barrister-s9q1.question: Which argument directly addresses a claim that a delivery was late?

answers.a1: The number of words in the contract title
answers.a2: A reliable delivery record showing the relevant date and time
answers.a4: A description of an unrelated delivery

barrister-s9q2.question: A strong argument contains a weak assumption. What improves it?

answers.a1: Repeat the conclusion more loudly
answers.a2: Hide the assumption from the reader
answers.a3: Test the assumption and address its limitations
answers.a4: Replace the evidence with confidence

barrister-s9q3.question: What is a concession in an argument?

answers.a1: Accepting a point while explaining its significance or limits
answers.a3: Refusing to address an opposing point
answers.a4: Changing a quotation without disclosure

barrister-s9q4.question: What is the problem with attacking a speaker’s appearance instead of their evidence?

answers.a1: It always proves the claim false
answers.a2: It does not address whether the evidence supports the claim
answers.a3: It replaces the need for relevant facts
answers.a4: It establishes the event’s date

barrister-s9q5.question: A quotation is accurate but omits a sentence that changes its meaning. What should be checked?

answers.a1: Whether the shortened version is more dramatic
answers.a4: Only the number of quotation marks

barrister-s9q6.question: Which statement expresses a limitation honestly?

answers.a1: “This record supports the date, but not who attended”
answers.a3: “Missing information can be assumed in our favour”
answers.a4: “This record proves every disputed fact”

barrister-s9q7.question: A conclusion goes beyond what the evidence shows. What is the best revision?

answers.a1: Describe the conclusion as certain without explanation
answers.a4: Narrow it to what the evidence can support

barrister-s10q1.question: A plan sets a goal but no way to check it. What is missing?

answers.a1: A suitable measure of progress
answers.a4: An unrelated deadline

barrister-s10q2.question: A decision is based on an old assessment, and circumstances have changed. What is needed?

answers.a1: A decision based on memory alone
answers.a3: Automatic repetition of the old decision
answers.a4: A review using current information

barrister-s10q3.question: What is a useful purpose of supervision or professional consultation?

answers.a1: To guarantee nobody can make a mistake
answers.a3: To avoid responsibility for every action
answers.a4: To reflect on difficult decisions and improve practice

barrister-s10q4.question: A task needs expertise you do not have. What is the appropriate response?

answers.a1: Choose the fastest answer regardless of risk
answers.a3: Seek suitable advice or referral within the process
answers.a4: Guess without disclosing uncertainty

barrister-s10q5.question: Two team members believe the other will make a follow-up call. What needs to be agreed?

answers.a1: Nothing; one will eventually guess
answers.a2: Only the title of the file
answers.a3: Who is responsible and when the action is due
answers.a4: Only which phone is newer

barrister-s10q6.question: A solution worked once. Does that guarantee it will fit every future case?

answers.a1: Yes; if the solution is easy to remember
answers.a2: Yes; one success establishes a universal rule
answers.a4: No; successful ideas can never be reused

barrister-s10q7.question: What makes feedback useful for improvement?

answers.a1: A claim that change is impossible
answers.a2: A personal insult with no example
answers.a4: Specific observations and a clear next step
